top_strength: The differentiator block is the strongest part of this call and she delivers it early, unprompted, right after the referral came up: the full No Worries pitch with the dollar figure, then "a few days before you move you'll receive a meet your mover email introducing them to you helping ease attention of strangers arriving at the front door," then the On-Time Guarantee, then a genuine open question — "do you have any specific concerns or questions that you want answered on this call in regards to your move?" That question is what surfaced that both customers are blind, which changed how the whole rest of the call needed to run, and she handled the disclosure without a beat of awkwardness. She was also proactively budget-conscious before being asked, steering the date herself: "that's actually one of our value days, so it's a bit cheaper to move on Tuesday through Thursday," and when the customer later asked, she had Friday and Saturday rates ready. The rapport is real, not performed — the kids-accumulate-stuff exchange and "black trash bag coming out" got a laugh, and the customer closed with "You've been really nice."
coaching_note: Finish the differentiators instead of listing their names. On-Time Guarantee landed as three words — "finally we do have an on time guarantee" — with no explanation of what it guarantees, and "no hidden fees" got asserted without the list behind it. Those are the two lines a customer actually repeats to a spouse, and both were left as headlines. Same pattern on the prep speech: she had the right instinct and the carload tip ("have the ability to take some of those small things over yourself in a car") but the consolidation half stayed abstract at "consolidate some things" — and on this specific call, where both customers are blind and are packing into totes themselves, naming what to consolidate (loose drawer items, photos off the walls, the toys) is worth real billed hours. These gaps read as habit, not tenure: the intake, pricing math, trip-fee explanation and booking mechanics are all clean and confident, which is the hard part. What is missing is the last sentence of scripts she already knows the first sentence of. Add one mechanical fix while you are at it — she used "Lily" once in twenty minutes on a call this warm.
phone_presence_notes: Genuine two-way rapport rather than affirmation-as-filler — she offered unprompted empathy ("I know moving is stressful"), responded to the customer's dog passing with "No, I'm sorry" before moving on, traded real stories about kids accumulating stuff, absorbed the blind-customer disclosure and the service-dog heads-up without any awkwardness, and the customer volunteered "You've been really nice" and asked for her name again at the end.
